The recorded Status='construction' (LastUpdated 2025-07-11) is stale and, on the evidence, was probably never really accurate for the Pakistani side. Timeline: Feb/Mar 2024 — Pakistan's CCoE approved building an 80km border-to-Gwadar segment ($158m) purely to avoid an Iranian breach claim, but land in Gwadar was never acquired and no construction followed (Dawn, world-energy.org, both Feb 2024). Nov 2024 — Iran filed an $18bn arbitration claim at the Paris ICC over Pakistan's non-construction (multiple outlets). Jan 2026 — three independent Pakistani/trade outlets, all url_verifier-confirmed, report Pakistan formally notifying Iran it intends to place the project on hold and pursue an out-of-court settlement to abandon it (digitalpakistan.pk, Jan 14 2026: 'Pakistan has formally conveyed to Iran that it intends to place the Iran-Pakistan (IP) gas pipeline project on hold'; pipeline-journal.net, Jan 15 2026: 'Pakistan has notified Iran of its intention to abandon the long-stalled Iran-Pakistan (IP) gas pipeline project through an out-of-court settlement'), while a parallel legal track (thenews.pk, Jan 23 2026) has Pakistan simultaneously requesting a 10-year extension to 2035 to avoid the $18bn arbitration penalty, with a verdict expected 2027-28 if no settlement is reached — i.e. Pakistan is hedging between abandonment and a decade-long extension, but under NEITHER track is actual construction proceeding. Both the 'abandon via settlement' and the '10-year extension' framings describe a project that is on the shelf, not under construction, so I'm proposing Status=shelved (ShelvedCancelledType=Confirmed, since this is an explicitly reported decision, not the mechanical dormancy rule) rather than 'cancelled' (Pakistan has explicitly left revival on the table, contingent on a US sanctions waiver) or 'proposed' (there IS an existing signed agreement and a built Iranian half, so 'proposed' understates it). NEWER, non-decisive signal: by April-June 2026, several outlets (Pakistan Today Apr 11 2026, ProPakistani, Express Tribune, Global Connectivities Jun 2026) report 'revival hopes rise' after US-Iran peace talks/an Islamabad-mediated ceasefire process, with an unnamed expert saying a sanctions rollback 'could create room to restart work' — but this is speculative/conditional language, not a report of construction actually resuming, so it does not change my verdict; it does mean this determination should be re-checked again soon given how fluid the situation is. [QC] ShelvedCancelledType 'Confirmed' -> 'confirmed' (live-column vocab).

Status=construction is still correct and remains actively evidenced, not stale. Chronology of dated, independent evidence: (1) 11 September 2024 -- ground broken on the Serhetabat(Turkmenistan)-Herat(Afghanistan) section, 'Arkadagyn ak yoly', the segment GEM's existing ConstructionYear=2024/ConstructionMonth=9 ref (worldpipelines.com) already covers; (2) 20 October 2025 -- Turkmenistan's Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov led a ceremony marking further progress on this 153km section, with Eurasianet and Times of Central Asia both independently reporting roughly 14km of pipe physically laid inside Afghanistan by that date; (3) 3 August 2026 (Ariana News, four days before this review) -- reports that Turkmenistan's government energy review for the first seven months of 2026 gave 'particular attention' to the Serhetabat-Herat section and stated 'work is being carried out in line with international standards.' No evidence found that construction has reached the Pakistan or India segments (per Jamestown and other analyses, those legs remain stalled pending India/Pakistan commercial and security decisions) -- this row is un-segmented (single sheet row for the whole international pipeline) so 'construction' correctly reflects that active, physical construction is genuinely underway on part of the line as of within the last week, even though the Pakistan/India legs have not broken ground. Recommend GEM consider whether this project would be better tracked with country-level segments (as it partly already is for the Iran-Pakistan comparator row), but that is a structural suggestion, not a status error.

Status=proposed is still correct. Most recent independent evidence: a July 2026 Russia-Pakistan bilateral relations tracker (russiaspivottoasia.com) describing the pipeline as one of the 'most ambitious long-term projects' with 'negotiations over its construction continuing between Moscow and Islamabad' -- i.e. still pre-agreement, not under construction. A May 2026 report (Times of Islamabad) similarly describes 'advancing technical and commercial negotiations' on the ~$3B project, with construction (~42 months) not yet begun. No source found reports FID, financial close, groundbreaking, or construction activity at any point 2024-2026; the project remains where it has been since the 2021 revised IGA -- a live, actively-discussed but not-yet-under-construction proposal, not dormant enough (this is under continuous active diplomatic engagement as recently as July 2026) to trigger the staleness/dormancy rule. See the separate StartYear1 spec flag in validity[] -- that date field is stale even though the Status value itself is not.

Timeline found: PITCO feasibility study for the Bahria Foundation LNG Terminal Project (Jul 2015-Mar 2017); ECC approval of the ISGS pipeline construction request (30 May 2018), reported by The Nation (19 Jun 2018); Exponent Engineers FEED review dated May 2018; Zameen News still describing the terminal as at the ECC-consideration stage in Mar 2019 (the most recent dated, independently-verifiable evidence I could find). I searched extensively (English and Urdu) for any 2020-2026 news on the Bahria Foundation Sonmiani LNG terminal or its Sonmiani-Nawabshah/Hub-Nawabshah pipeline -- found nothing: no completion, construction-start, cancellation, or revival story, and no mention in any of the Gwadar-Nawabshah-project revival coverage (that is a separate, unrelated project). ISGS's own site (isgs.com.pk) is Cloudflare-blocked to both WebFetch and curl; its Wayback Machine captures for the relevant project-gallery pages only preserved the site's homepage shell, not gallery content, so I could not check ISGS's own current project list. Engineering-firm portfolio pages (Exponent, PITCO) describing 'FEED completed'/'under development' are undated relative to today and read as legacy 2018-era project descriptions, not current updates. Given the current recorded Status is already 'shelved' and there is no independent evidence of any activity in roughly 7 years (since the 2019 evidence), this satisfies the 'shelved >=4y -> cancelled' dormancy rule. Presumed inference only -- no fabricated ref, per standing rule 2. [QC] ShelvedCancelledType 'Presumed' -> 'inferred' (live-column vocab).

Timeline of real progress: Jun-2018 MOU -> Feb-2019 inter-corporate agreement -> Gazprom's feasibility study originally slated to START Q1-2020 and finish within one year (Gulf Times). No source anywhere reports feasibility-study results, a financing close, or any construction milestone for THIS specific offshore/undersea project. The most recent substantive mention found is Warsaw Institute, 30-Sep-2022, which says only that 'a sea link between the offshore pipeline and the Pakistan Stream gas pipeline is now being considered' -- i.e. still speculative, no progress. A Feb-2023 Pipeline Technology Journal piece on reviving the North-South/Pakistan Stream project via Gwadar mentions an 'abandoned Gwadar LNG Pipeline Project' connecting to Iran, run by ISGS + Chinese firms -- this appears to be a RELATED BUT DISTINCT entity (an LNG-import + onshore pipe concept, not clearly the same as Gazprom's $10bn undersea line), so I have not merged it in, but it reinforces that the broader 'Gwadar seaborne gas import' concept had stalled by 2023. Broader Pakistan-Russia energy news through 2024-2025 (e.g. Gazprom/Novatek LNG talks, Portovaya/Ust-Luga LNG cooperation) has shifted entirely to LNG supply rather than this pipeline, with no mention of the offshore line being revived. Iran's own onshore IP pipeline (P0452) was separately reported abandoned by Pakistan in Aug-2023 over US-sanctions risk (Middle East Monitor), removing much of the rationale for an Iran-sourced offshore alternative too. With no independent evidence of activity since ~Sep-2022 (roughly 4 years dormant as of Aug-2026), the 2-year proposed-with-no-progress dormancy rule applies: propose Status=shelved, ShelvedCancelledType=Presumed, no fabricated ref per standing rule 2. [QC] ShelvedCancelledType 'Presumed' -> 'inferred' (live-column vocab).

Recorded Status='construction' with StartYear1=2025 (i.e. a still-future start) does not survive a check against SNGPL's own current corporate reporting. SNGPL's FY2025 Annual Report puts the near-identical project (16"-42" dia x 762km 'Qadirpur-Lahore Pipeline' + 25,000HP compression, 'gas downstream Sawan up to Lahore') on its p.76 'Milestones' page — a page of completed historical achievements (confirmed by TOC entry '76 Milestones' and by every neighboring entry being past-tense: Phase II 'was undertaken to transport additional 400 MMCFD RLNG downstream Sawan', Phase IV 'was laid for supply of RLNG to Power Plants i.e. Bhikki, Balloki, Haveli Bahadur Shah and Nandipur'). That Phase IV entry names the exact four RLNG power plants this trunk feeds. Independently, nsenergybusiness.com's Bhikki project page confirms the plant draws RLNG via an 18km spur off 'SNGPL's Qilla Sattar Shah to Bhikki pipeline' — Qilla Sattar Shah being the precise near-Lahore terminus named in the original 2017 sanction reporting for THIS pipeline (offshore-energy.biz: '42-inch pipeline from Sawan to Qilla Satar Shah, near Lahore, 780km'). And Dawn (Nov 2017) reports LNG-terminal-maintenance supply curtailments actually being applied to Bhikki/Balloki/Haveli Bahadur Shah/Nandipur with specific MMCFD figures — i.e. gas was demonstrably flowing to these plants via this network by November 2017. Three independent sources (SNGPL itself, an industry trade outlet, a national newspaper), none tracing to GEM or to each other, converge on: this trunk was built and moving RLNG by 2017, not merely 'under construction' toward a 2025 start that has by now already passed without incident in any source I found. I'm proposing StartYear1=2017 as the best-evidenced anchor (Dawn's Nov-2017 evidence of active flow) rather than a precise commissioning month, which I could not pin down further; a human should ideally cross-check against SNGPL's earlier (e.g. FY2017-18) annual report for an exact commissioning date/month before finalizing. Tier=high on the strength of three independent, differently-sourced confirmations; residual uncertainty is only about the EXACT month of the status change, not the direction of it. Did not attempt a staleness-rule demotion (the dormancy rules in the SOP apply to proposed/shelved decay, not to this situation, which is a positive-evidence upgrade, not a decay inference).

resolutions.recommendation: No action — existence, commodity, classification, and duplicate checks all pass.
resolutions.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: real, heavily documented, 15+ years of coverage in independent outlets across two countries (Reuters, The Diplomat, NPR, Dawn, VOA, Al Jazeera, Pakistan Today, ISSI, ICWA, dozens more). Iran's ~1,150km domestic section was physically completed years ago (NIOC/Ministry of Petroleum investment); the Pakistani ~780km section was formally inaugurated in 2013 (Zardari/Ahmadinejad ceremony) and has an approved-but-unbuilt 80km Gwadar-border segment (Pakistan CCoE, Feb/Mar 2024). This is not a GEM-only/hallucinated entity. CLASSIFICATION: Fuel=Gas and PipelineType=transmission are both correct — every independent source describes a large-diameter (56in) international transmission trunk carrying South Pars gas into Pakistan's national grid, not a gathering/feeder line. DUPLICATE: checked against the full 6-row Pakistan-gas roster — P0766 (TAPI, a different quadrilateral project via Afghanistan), P3101 (Pakistan Stream, Karachi-based, a separate Russia-linked proposal), P3173 (Somiani-Nawabshah, a purely domestic Balochistan-Sindh line unrelated to Iran), P3174 (Off-Shore, undefined endpoints) and P3178 (Sawan-Lahore, a domestic Sindh-Punjab trunk). None of these describe the Iran-to-Pakistan international corridor; P0452 is not a relabel/segment-double-count of any of them.

resolutions.researcher_notes: The sheet records StartYear1=2024 with no ref (MISSING_REF). I could not verify that construction actually began in 2024. What independently verifies: Pakistan's caretaker cabinet (CCoE) approved, on Feb 24 2024 and again Mar 29 2024, a plan to build an 80km border-to-Gwadar segment ($158m) specifically to avoid an Iranian breach claim (Dawn, world-energy.org, both dated Feb 2024). But by the time of Iran's Nov 2024 arbitration filing at the Paris ICC ($18bn claim) and subsequent reporting through Jan 2026, no source reports land acquisition, groundbreaking, or any pipe laid on the Pakistani side — one search summary explicitly states 'the land in Gwadar earmarked for construction has yet to be acquired.' 2024 therefore looks like the year of a paper/cabinet approval, not an actual construction start, and by 2026 Pakistan is formally trying to abandon/settle the project rather than build it (see status_reviews). Recommend treating StartYear1=2024 as unverified/likely incorrect for an actual physical start.

resolutions.researcher_notes: Owner1 = 'Iran Ministry of Petroleum' at 100% is recorded with no ref (MISSING_REF). Independent sources consistently describe a two-sided ownership structure: Iran's National Iranian Oil Company (under the Ministry of Petroleum) built and owns the ~1,150km Iranian section; Pakistan's Inter State Gas Systems (ISGS, a wholly state-owned company under the Petroleum Division) is the counterparty responsible for financing/building/owning the Pakistani ~780km section (Wikipedia: 'In Pakistan, InterState Gas Systems manages construction'; world-energy.org, Feb 2024, names ISGS as the entity NIOC served its Dec 2023 breach notice on). A single 100%-Iran owner record describes only the built (Iranian) portion and omits Pakistan's own stake/liability in its unbuilt segment. This is a caveat, not a hard error, since GEM may be scoping ownership to the entity that actually built physical asset to date.

resolutions.recommendation: Length, diameter and capacity values pass corroboration but carry cross-source caveats worth a note in ResearcherNotes: (1) length has a genuine, unresolved cross-source conflict; (2) diameter reflects only the built Iranian section.
resolutions.researcher_notes: CAPACITY (750 MMcf/d): independently confirmed — world-energy.org (Feb 19 2024, genuinely separate origin) quotes the original 2009 supply agreement as '750 MMCFD for 25 years from South Pars,' matching the existing offshore-technology.com ref exactly; note offshore-technology.com and oilandgasadvancement.com share identical boilerplate wording (same GlobalData/Verdict-Media project-database network) so they count as ONE source for corroboration purposes, not two — world-energy.org is the genuinely independent second leg. DIAMETER (56in): confirmed as the Iranian section's diameter (offshore-technology.com, matches existing ref) and is the figure universally quoted as 'the' pipeline diameter, but multiple sources (Wikipedia; offshore-technology.com itself) note the still-unbuilt Pakistani section is designed for a narrower 42in pipe — 56in is accurate for what's actually built, worth a note that it's Iran-side spec. LENGTH (2,775km): matches the commonly repeated headline total (Wikipedia's stated total; The Diplomat, the existing ref). However there is a real, unresolved conflict across sources: the offshore-technology.com/oilandgasadvancement.com network states an internally-consistent total of 1,880km (1,100km Iran + 780km Pakistan), and even Wikipedia's own segment breakdown (1,172km Iran + 785km Pakistan = 1,957km) doesn't sum to its own stated 2,775km total. 2,775km is still the most-repeated figure across sources including the sheet's own existing ref, so I'm not proposing a change, but flagging that GEM's number does not have a clean, fully-reconciled cross-source derivation.

resolutions.recommendation: no action needed on existence/classification/duplicate; this is the well-documented TAPI megaproject, correctly classified as a gas transmission trunk, and not a duplicate of any other roster row
resolutions.researcher_notes: This row is the TAPI (Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India) pipeline, one of the most heavily and independently documented gas megaprojects in the world -- ADB (project financier/facilitator), the Turkmenistan and Afghan foreign/mining ministries, Asian Development Bank project pages, Oil & Gas Journal, Eurasianet, World Pipelines, and dozens of press outlets all track it under this exact name and route, entirely independent of GEM. Existence is not in doubt. Classification (Fuel=Gas, PipelineType=transmission) is correct -- it is explicitly an international gas-export trunk line, not a gathering/feeder line. Checked against the 6-pipeline roster for this batch: P0452 (Iran-Pakistan Pipeline) is a wholly separate project (different supply source -- South Pars, Iran -- different route, different sponsors) and none of the other 4 rows (P3101 Pakistan Stream, P3173 Somiani-Nawabshah, P3174 Off-Shore, P3178 Sawan-Lahore) describe the same corridor or endpoints as TAPI, so no duplicate/relabel concern. Spec values LengthKnown=1814 km, Diameter=56 in, and Capacity=33 bcm/y are all independently corroborated by multiple non-GEM sources (Offshore Technology project page, Wikipedia TAPI Pipeline article, NS Energy Business project page) -- no material disagreement found on those three. CAVEAT: SegmentCost=$7,000,000,000 USD sits inside a genuinely volatile literature -- ADB's original 2005 estimate was $7.6bn, it later blew out toward $10bn, was reportedly cut ~30% to $7bn in Nov 2018, and a 2020 estimate cited $7.7bn; but two independently-sourced, more recent overview pages (Oil & Gas Journal's retrospective and NS Energy Business's project profile) both currently state the cost as $10bn, not $7bn. That is a real, material (~40%) disagreement between GEM's figure and the currently-cited figure in reputable secondary sources, so I did NOT add a ref for SegmentCost as a confirmation -- see the paired validity/spec concern below and the UNRESOLVED fill entry.

resolutions.recommendation: correct StartState/Province from 'Ahal' to 'Mary' (the Turkmenistan-side origin/border-crossing point and the Galkynysh gas field itself are both in Mary Province, not Ahal Province)
resolutions.researcher_notes: GEM's Location [ref] cluster records StartCountryOrArea=Turkmenistan / StartState/Province=Ahal. This is wrong. Four independent sources place both the Galkynysh gas field (the pipeline's stated FuelSource, itself correct) and Serhetabat -- the actual Turkmenistan border town/pipeline crossing point into Afghanistan -- in Mary Province (velayat), not Ahal Province: (1) Wikipedia's Galkynysh Gas Field article states the field is 'near Yoloten in Mary Province of Turkmenistan'; (2) Wikipedia's Serhetabat article states it 'is a city in Tagtabazar District, Mary Province, Turkmenistan ... bordering Afghanistan'; (3) Offshore Technology's TAPI project page states the pipeline 'begins in the Mary region of Turkmenistan'; (4) Turkmenistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs news release on the pipeline's construction launch states it explicitly: 'On 11 September 2024, in the Mary province ... the construction of a key segment of the TAPI pipeline -- the Serhetabat-Herat section ... was launched.' Ahal Province is the central Turkmenistan province around the capital Ashgabat, geographically distinct from Mary Province in the southeast where the field and the border crossing actually sit. EndLocation/EndState-Province/EndCountryOrArea (Fazilka, Punjab, India) are independently confirmed correct by the same Offshore Technology page and by Wikipedia's TAPI Pipeline article, so only the start province needs correction.

resolutions.recommendation: flag SegmentCost=$7,000,000,000 for review -- currently-cited overview sources say $10bn; do not silently overwrite, the cost figure has genuinely moved across multiple published estimates over 20 years
resolutions.researcher_notes: See the caveat noted in the first validity entry. Oil & Gas Journal's TAPI retrospective states plainly that 'persistent delays have since raised TAPI's projected cost to $10 billion' (up from ADB's 2005 estimate of $7.6bn, itself up from a 2002 estimate of $2.6bn), and NS Energy Business's project profile independently lists 'Estimated Investment: $10bn.' Those are two independent, reasonably current sources that disagree with GEM's $7bn figure by a material margin. There IS a documented $7bn figure in the literature (a Nov 2018 announcement that project costs were cut ~30% to $7bn, with a 2020 estimate of $7.7bn), so GEM's number is not fabricated or baseless -- it likely reflects that 2018/2020 vintage -- but given more recent sources cite $10bn, I'm flagging this as a genuine spec disagreement rather than confirming or silently filling it. Left SegmentCost unresolved rather than proposing a value change (a real research judgment call, not mechanical).

resolutions.researcher_notes: gem.wiki was 403/Cloudflare-blocked this run (wiki_citations.json empty for this scope), so I went straight to open-web research per the scope note. EXISTENCE: real, independently confirmed. The Pakistan ECC (Economic Coordination Committee) approved, on 30 May 2018, a request by Bahria Foundation (a Pakistan Navy welfare trust) for Interstate Gas Systems (ISGS, a Government Holdings/Petroleum Division subsidiary -- matches GEM's Parent field) to construct a pipeline from the proposed Bahria Foundation LNG terminal at Sonmiani (Lasbela district, Balochistan) to Nawabshah (Sindh), reported in detail by The Nation (19 Jun 2018, https://www.nation.com.pk/19-Jun-2018/govt-to-lay-310km-pipeline-to-connect-lng-terminal-with-nawabshah -- verified OK, contains '310', 'Nawabshah', '1200'). A second, independent outlet (Zameen News, 27 Mar 2019, https://www.zameen.com/news/bahria-foundation-may-establish-lng-terminal.html -- verified OK) separately corroborates the Bahria Foundation LNG terminal at Sonmiani being tied into a 'Hub-Nawabshah gas pipeline project', confirming the project's existence and route concept from a different origin, though it gives no exact length/capacity figures. Two supporting (non-cited, engineering-firm portfolio) pages -- Exponent Engineers' FEED review and PITCO's feasibility-study page for the Bahria Foundation LNG Terminal Project -- corroborate the terminal side of the project but describe only a short (~7km, 32-inch) SUBSEA line to shore, which is a DIFFERENT, shorter segment than this 310km onshore trunk to Nawabshah -- I did not use their pipe diameter for this row to avoid conflating the two segments. CLASSIFICATION: correct. The Nation article describes a full transmission-grade system (metering station, main-line block valve stations, receiving stations, cathodic protection, SCADA, river/canal/railway crossings, 40-year design life) crossing multiple provinces -- a transmission trunk, not a gathering/feeder line; Fuel=Gas is correct (it carries regasified LNG as pipeline-quality natural gas). DUPLICATE: checked against the 6-row Pakistan-gas roster. Not a duplicate of P0452 (Iran-Pakistan, different corridor/endpoints), P0766 (TAPI, ends in Punjab), P3101 (Pakistan Stream, Karachi-based), P3174 (Off-Shore Gas Pipeline, len=1500/cap=1000 -- close in concept, since ISGS's own site lists a distinct 'OSGP' project, but the numbers and stated route don't match this row and I found no source tying them together -- flagging as worth a second look but not calling it a duplicate on current evidence), or P3178 (Sawan-Lahore, different origin field). Also confirmed this is NOT the separate, much larger 'Gwadar-Nawabshah' LNG/pipeline project (Rs203bn/US$2bn, ISGS-CNPC, ~700km) that recurs heavily in search results under a similar name -- that is a different corridor (Gwadar, not Sonmiani/Hub) and is not in the current roster. ATTRIBUTION: Owner1=Interstate Gas Systems 100% confirmed by the Nation article ('ISGS would construct and operate the pipeline'); StartLocation/Province (Sonmiani/Balochistan) and EndLocation/Province (Nawabshah/Sindh) confirmed by both sources. Minor caveat: the Nation article's actual route detail says the pipe runs 'Hub to Dureji (158km)' then 'Dureji to Nawabshah (152km)' -- Hub is the nearby town/district seat serving Sonmiani Bay, not a literal renaming, so I don't read this as an endpoint error, just a precision note for whoever routes this in the geometry tool. SPEC: LengthKnown=310km and Capacity=1200 MMcf/d both match the Nation article's '310 km' and 'capable of transporting 700 to 1200 MMCFD' (GEM recorded the range's ceiling, a defensible choice). Because only one outlet gives the exact numbers, I'm scoring the length/capacity/owner fills tier=medium (single strong, government-approval-sourced article) even though existence itself is tier=high (2 independent outlets). Diameter is correctly left blank -- no source gives a diameter for the 310km trunk specifically (only for the unrelated 7km subsea segment).

resolutions.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: real, well-documented proposal, distinct from every other roster row. Feb 2019: Pakistan's Inter State Gas Systems (ISGS, state-owned) and Russia's Gazprom PJSC signed an inter-corporate agreement (following a June 2018 MOU) for a >1,500 km, $10bn UNDERSEA/offshore gas pipeline landing at Gwadar, part of a wider $14bn Gazprom package that also covered the separate Pakistan Stream / North-South line ($2.5bn) and gas storage ($1.5bn). Corroborated independently by thenews.com.pk (7-Feb-2019, the sheet's own already-cited Length/SegmentCost source, recovered via Wayback since the live page now 403s), Russia Business Today, Warsaw Institute (two separate articles, 2019 and 2022), Asia Times (Jul-2019), Gulf Times, and Profit/Pakistan Today (Jun-2018) -- all independent outlets, all describing the SAME $10bn/1,500km/Gwadar project, not a wire reprint. CLASSIFICATION: Fuel=Gas and PipelineType=transmission are both correct -- every source describes a large trunk import line, not a gathering/process line. DUPLICATE: checked against the full 6-row Pakistan-gas roster. NOT the same pipe as P3101 (Pakistan Stream/North-South: $2.5bn, ~1,100-1,122 km, Karachi Port Qasim -> Lahore/Kasur, onshore) -- every source treats the offshore project and Pakistan Stream as two separate line items in the same Gazprom package, with different costs and different lengths, and even mentions a possible future 'sea link' BETWEEN the two (Warsaw Institute, Sep-2022) that confirms they are not the same object. NOT the same pipe as P0452 (the classic onshore Iran-Pakistan 'Peace' pipeline, Asaluyeh->Sindh, 2,775 km) -- P3174 is the Gazprom-brokered undersea ALTERNATIVE route via Gwadar (Asia Times, Jul-2019: 'the gas volume allocated for the IP gas pipeline project would be diverted to the offshore gas pipeline project'), a materially different length/cost/sponsor. ATTRIBUTION CAVEAT (the one real finding): sources disagree on which country's gas actually feeds the pipeline. Warsaw Institute (x2), Asia Times, and Gulf Times all name IRAN as (at least one of) the source country/fields, matching the sheet's current EndCountryOrArea=Iran. But the earliest, most specific, on-the-record report -- thenews.com.pk, 7-Feb-2019, quoting the signing officials directly, and already cited by the sheet for Length/SegmentCost -- states the gas would come from 'Gazprom's sources in the Middle East,' naming 'Bahrain, Qatar and other Middle Eastern countries' and never mentioning Iran. Gulf-Times splits the difference ('gas deposits in Iran and in other Middle East countries'). So 'Iran' has more independent naming instances (3 outlets) than 'Qatar/Bahrain' (1 outlet, albeit the most authoritative direct-quote piece), but no single source is unambiguous and none of this ever reached a final, sourced route -- flag as an open attribution question rather than a settled fact. SPEC: Length 1,500 km confirmed verbatim by 2 independent sources (thenews.com.pk: 'more than 1,500 km'; Russia Business Today: 'over 1,500 km'). Cost $10bn confirmed by 5+ independent sources. Capacity 1000 MMcf/d matches the upper end of the range every source gives ('500 million to one billion cubic feet of gas per day') -- consistent, not contradicted. OWNER: Gazprom PJSC is correctly named as the Russian corporate counterpart (thenews.com.pk names the signatory as 'Vitaly A Markelov ... PJSC Gazprom International'), but the recorded Owner1%=100.00% is an unconfirmed convention value -- this MOU never reached FID and no equity/ownership structure for an actual pipeline entity has ever been announced (contrast with Pakistan Stream/P3101, where a 74%/26% Pakistan/Russia split IS reported). STATUS OF THE STATUS REF: the sheet's Status[ref] (warsawinstitute.org 'Russia Enters the Pakistan Gas Sector') is live (200) and does substantively support 'proposed'/feasibility-stage even though it doesn't contain the literal word 'proposed' -- the worklist's automated flag on this is a false negative, not a real support gap.

resolutions.researcher_notes: The recorded Status='construction' with StartYear1=2025 looks stale/wrong, not just unsourced. SNGPL's own FY2025 Annual Report (sngpl.com.pk/download/AnnualReport-2025/SNGPLAR2025.pdf), on its p.76 'Milestones' page (a historical-achievements timeline, NOT a future-plans page — confirmed by the table of contents entry '76 Milestones' and by every other entry on that page being past-tense completed work), lists 'PROJECT X (PHASE III): 16"-42" dia x 762 KM long Qadirpur–Lahore Pipeline along with installation of 25,000 HP Compression [to transport] gas downstream Sawan up to Lahore' as a completed item, immediately adjacent to 'PROJECT X (PHASE IV): 30"/24" dia x 149 KM long spurs...for supply of RLNG to Power Plants i.e. Bhikki, Balloki, Haveli Bahadur Shah and Nandipur' (also completed). This matches GEM's P3178 almost exactly on route (Sawan/Qadirpur→Lahore), diameter ceiling (42in), and stated purpose (RLNG transport downstream of Sawan) — GEM's 770km sits inside the 750–780km band every source uses for this same corridor (see the confirmed-caveat entry below). Independently, nsenergybusiness.com's Bhikki power-plant page states the plant's RLNG 'is supplied...through an 18km spur gas pipeline connected with SNGPL's Qilla Sattar Shah to Bhikki pipeline' — Qilla Sattar Shah near Lahore is the exact terminus named in the original 2017 sanction press (offshore-energy.biz: '42-inch pipeline from Sawan to Qilla Satar Shah, near Lahore (780km)'), confirming that trunk is built and live. Further independently, Dawn (dawn.com/news/1368494, Nov 2017) reports LNG-terminal maintenance forcing supply curtailments to Bhikki, Haveli Bahadur Shah, Balloki and Nandipur ('85MMCFD is being supplied to Balloki, Nandipur-31MMCFD' etc.) — i.e. these plants were already drawing RLNG through this network by November 2017, years before GEM's recorded 2025 start. Three independent, non-GEM sources (SNGPL's own corporate report, an industry trade outlet, and a national newspaper) converge on the same conclusion: the trunk is built and has been moving RLNG since 2017–18, not 'under construction' toward a still-future 2025 start. Filed as a spec/status concern rather than existence — the pipeline unquestionably exists; what's wrong is the lifecycle stage recorded for it. Full sourcing/verdict in the status_reviews array below (do not also treat this as a fill for Status[ref] or Start[ref] — those are marked UNRESOLVED, not confirmed, since I am NOT supporting the current values).

resolutions.recommendation: Re-derive SegmentCost — the currently recorded $672,000,000 USD does not reconcile with the sourced PKR figure at a contemporaneous exchange rate; flag for correction rather than pasting a ref that would falsely appear to confirm it.
resolutions.researcher_notes: The original sanction press (offshore-energy.biz, 6 Mar 2017, verified OK; also reported by Express Tribune 2017, verified via Wayback) states the total investment as 'PKR 110.5 billion (approximately US$1 billion)' for this exact project (1,200mmcfd capacity, Sawan–Qilla Satar Shah stage). PKR110.51bn at the 2017 exchange rate (~PKR104–105/USD) is ~US$1.05–1.06 billion — consistent with the source's own 'approximately US$1 billion' gloss. GEM's recorded SegmentCost of $672,000,000 implies an effective rate of ~PKR164/USD, which is a mid-2022/2023-era rate, not a 2017 one. This looks like a currency-conversion-year mismatch (the PKR figure converted at a much-later, post-devaluation rate rather than the rate contemporaneous with the 2017 sanction), the same class of defect already logged elsewhere in this project as a length-units/exchange-rate hazard. I could not find an independent, more recent PKR figure that would justify $672M as a genuinely lower re-estimated cost (no cost-overrun-reduction or re-scoping story turned up), so I'm not proposing a replacement number — just flagging the number as unreconciled and worth a human re-check of the original entry's conversion math. Leaving SegmentCost [ref] UNRESOLVED rather than fabricating support for a value I believe is arithmetically off.
